newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Baltic premiers to make special EU declaration.
newsitem.headline: Baltic premiers to make special EU declaration.

text.p: The prime ministers of the three Baltic states plan to sign a joint declaration reaffirming their countries' readiness to join the European Union (EU), the Lithuanian premier's office said on Wednesday.
The declaration will be signed on June 12, days before EU leaders are to meet at a June 16-17 summit in Amsterdam to decide reforms to pave the way for taking in new members.
Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have all applied for EU membership, seeking to cement ties with the West after regaining independence from the former Soviet Union in 1991.

The statement will be signed during a meeting in the Estonian capital Tallinn by Lithuanian Prime Minister Gediminas Vagnorius, Latvia's Andris Shkele and Estonian Prime Minister Mart Siimann, the press office said in a statement.

"The wording of the proposed text is that we declare that Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have accomplished a lot in European harmonisation as well as forming market economies," an adviser to Vagnorius told Reuters.
"We will declare that we are ready to start accession negotiations as soon as possible," the adviser added.
The Baltic states, which spent five decades as unwilling Soviet republics, are generally regarded as the star reformers of the former Soviet Union.
All three have made rapid strides in the transition to a market economy, liberalising prices and pushing privatisation.
But they worry that there may be a lack of political commitment in the West to take in their small countries, which have a combined population of just eight million, in a first wave of EU growth.

Nordic EU members voice strong support for Baltic entry but leading EU nations such as Germany and France, while sympathetic to the Balts, have appeared more concerned to secure entry for central European states such as Poland and the Czech Republic.
The Balts have also applied to join NATO but strong Russian objections are likely to block any early entry.

Some Western analysts have called for at least one Baltic country to enter the EU. This would be a reward for their reform efforts and as a way of boosting their security as they remain deeply suspicious of Russia, which has ruled them for most of the last 200 years.
